newsitem.title: THAILAND: FOCUS - Siam Cement hit by slow economy, oversupply.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Siam Cement hit by slow economy, oversupply.

text.p: Thailand's largest industrial conglomerate and cement producer, Siam Cement Plc, is expected to post slower earnings growth this year, hurt by the country's severely flagging economy, analysts said on Wednesday.
The government's move to tighten spending on infrastructure projects will also adversely affect the firm by reducing demand for cement and building materials from the public sector.
"We are in the process of revising down the company's profit in 1997 from previous projection of 7.5 billion baht," an analyst at Capital Nomura Securities told Reuters.
"The sluggish economy and government's tightening budget spending will really affect the company," he said.
Siam Cement on Wednesday announced a 29 percent fall in its first quarter consolidated profit of 1.91 billion baht from 2.71 billion baht in the same quarter last year.

The group's poor first quarter profit which was significantly lower than the market's expectation prompted a selloff on the heavy-weighted shares and dragged down the SET composite index, analysts said.
Merrill Lynch on Wednesday projected Siam Cement would post a consolidated net profit of two billion baht in the first quarter, down 23 percent from the same period a year ago.
"Investors weren't happy with the weak earnings of Siam Cement," said Thanawat Patchimkul, an analyst at Seamico Securities.
Siam Cement closed down eight baht to 528 after dipping to a day low of 514.

Siam Cement president Chumpol Na Lamliang said the sharp drop in the group's earnings in the first quarter was due to higher administrative and selling expenses as well as lower foreign exchange gains following recent baht weakness.
Chumpol said the group's sales growth this year was expected to be at around 5-10 percent which will be lower than its original forecast of 15 percent.

An oversupply of cement this year would also take a toll on the company's earnings as the capacity expansion of local cement producers would exceed the domestic demand already hit by depressed property sector and the slow public spending on infrastructure projects.
The research house Vickers Ballas said in a new report that there will be an estimated 7.4 million tonnes of cement surplus in this year.
"We think the chance for an increase in cement price is very unlikely. On the contrary, a lower selling price is more reasonable as competition intensifies," Vickers Ballas said.
Cement business contributes about 40 percent to Siam Cement's consolidated profit, analysts said.
